passages.happening:
Paul has just said that he speaks with sincerity, as a man sent from God. Now he stops himself. Will they think he is praising himself again? “Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you?” (verse 1).

He does not need such letters. The church itself is his letter. “You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone” (verse 2).

Then Paul turns the picture. “It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Letters of recommendation were part of ordinary life in the Greek and Roman world. A person travelling to a strange city, or seeking a hearing, would carry a letter from someone known and trusted, saying who the bearer was and asking that he be welcomed. Many such letters survive on papyrus, the paper of the ancient world. They usually say something good about the bearer and then make a request. In a city like Corinth, where status and patrons mattered, such a letter showed whom you were connected to.

The churches used them too. When Apollos went to Achaia, “the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him” (Acts 18:27). Paul himself writes a short recommendation for Phoebe at the end of Romans (Romans 16:1-2).

So Paul is not against such letters. But it seems that rival teachers had come to Corinth carrying impressive letters, and some were asking why Paul had none. Paul's answer is that he started the church. The changed lives of the Corinthians are his proof. Anyone in the city could read that ‘letter’.

Then he says something deeper. The real author is Christ, not Paul. Paul only delivered it. And it is written not with ink, which fades, but by the Spirit of God, on human hearts.
passages.ot:
‘Tablets of stone’ points to Mount Sinai. God gave Moses “the two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18).

‘Tablets of human hearts’ points to the prophets' promise of something new. Through Jeremiah God said of a coming covenant, “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Through Ezekiel God said, “I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put My Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

Paul is saying that this promise has begun to come true in Corinth. The Spirit is writing God's ways into the lives of ordinary believers.
passages.asks: Paul says the Corinthians are a letter that everyone can read. Ask what a neighbour or a coworker would read in your life, or in your church's life. And ask whose approval you look for: the right connections and credentials, or the quiet work of God's Spirit in people.

passages.t: Letter and Spirit, the old covenant and the new
passages.happening:
Paul is confident, but not in himself. “Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God” (verse 5). This answers the question of 2:16, ‘who is qualified?’.

God has made him a servant of something new. “And He has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (verse 6).

Then Paul compares the two covenants. The law given at Sinai came with glory. It was so bright “that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses because of its fleeting glory” (verse 7). If that ministry had glory, “will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?” (verse 8).

He says the same thing three ways. If a ministry that brought condemnation had glory, how much more the one that brings righteousness (verse 9). What once had glory has none by comparison with the greater glory (verse 10). “For if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of that which endures!” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
A covenant is a binding promise between God and his people. The ‘old covenant’ is the one God made with Israel at Sinai, when he gave the law. The ‘new covenant’ is the one God promised through Jeremiah, and which Jesus spoke of at the Last Supper: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20).

‘The letter’ is the Greek gramma, something written. Here it means the law as written words, carved on stone. ‘The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.’ Paul does not mean that the law is bad. In Romans he says, “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12). He means that written commands, on their own, cannot change a heart. They show what is right, and so they show where people fall short. That leads to condemnation. The Spirit does what the written words could not: he gives new life from within.

Some readers have taken ‘the letter kills’ as a rule for reading the Bible, as if Paul meant that its plain sense is dead and only hidden meanings give life. Most readers today think that is not his point. Paul is comparing two covenants, not two ways of reading a page.

Notice how Paul argues. ‘If this, how much more that.’ Jewish teachers often argued from the lesser to the greater in just this way. Paul does it three times. And every time, he grants that the old covenant had real glory. He is not saying the law was worthless. He is saying the new is greater.

‘Fleeting glory’ and ‘fading away’ translate one Greek word, katargeō. It can mean to fade, or to be brought to an end, or to be set aside. Exodus does not say that the shine on Moses' face faded. Paul seems to be reading the whole story in the light of what came after: the glory of Sinai was real, but it was not meant to be the last word.
passages.ot:
The story behind these verses is Exodus 34. When Moses came down from the mountain with the law, “he was unaware that his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD” (Exodus 34:29). The people “were afraid to approach him” (Exodus 34:30).

The promise of a new covenant is Jeremiah's. “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31). It would not be like the old one, which the people had broken. God would write his law on their hearts and forgive their sins (Jeremiah 31:33-34).

The Old Testament itself longed for the heart to be changed. Moses promised, “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

And the Psalms celebrate the law's glory. “The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7). Paul does not deny it. He says the Spirit gives what the law pointed to.
passages.hard:
Does ‘the letter kills’ mean the Old Testament law is bad, or that Christians can set it aside?

No. Paul calls the law glorious in these very verses, and elsewhere holy and good. His point is that written commands alone could not give life. ‘The letter’ is the law as an outside rule, carved on stone. The Spirit writes God's will on the heart. Paul is not telling anyone to ignore Scripture or to read it loosely. In Romans he asks, “Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law” (Romans 3:31).

Christians do differ on exactly how the law of Moses applies to believers today, which commands still bind and how. But on every view, the Old Testament remains Christian Scripture. Paul says the Corinthians' new life is written ‘by the Spirit of the living God’, the same God who gave the law.
passages.asks: Paul says his competence comes from God. Ask where you have been relying on your own ability, and where you need God's. Then ask whether you know God's commands only as rules on the outside, or whether his Spirit is writing them on your heart. What would change if he were?

passages.happening:
Because the new covenant has such hope, Paul says, “we are very bold” (verse 12). He speaks openly.

Moses, Paul says, covered his face: “We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away” (verse 13).

Then Paul turns the veil into a picture. “But their minds were closed. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed” (verse 14). “And even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts” (verse 15).

But the veil can go. “But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (verse 16).

“Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (verse 17).

And Paul ends with all believers. “And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
In Exodus, Moses took the veil off when he went in to speak with the LORD, and put it back on when he spoke to the people. Paul uses that veil as a picture of a covering over the mind and heart that keeps a reader from seeing where the Scriptures lead.

‘When Moses is read’ means the reading of the books of Moses. In the synagogue they were read aloud every Sabbath. James says in Acts, “Moses has been proclaimed in every city from ancient times and is read in the synagogues on every Sabbath” (Acts 15:21).

Paul himself had read Moses that way for years, as a strict Pharisee. Then, on the road to Damascus, he met the risen Jesus, and he came to read the same Scriptures as pointing to Christ. When he speaks of the veil, he is speaking of what was once true of himself.

Verse 16 is almost a quotation of Exodus. Moses ‘went in before the LORD’ and removed the veil. Paul says that whenever anyone, Jew or Gentile, ‘turns to the Lord’, the veil is taken away.

‘The Lord is the Spirit’ is a puzzling phrase. Some read it as Paul explaining Exodus: the LORD whom Moses met face to face is met now through the Spirit. Others read it as saying that the risen Lord is present among his people by his Spirit. Neither reading erases the difference between Christ and the Spirit, since the very next words speak of ‘the Spirit of the Lord’.

‘Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.’ In this setting the freedom is first of all freedom from the veil: freedom to come to God with nothing in between, and to be changed by him. It is not a freedom to do as one likes. Paul tells another church, “do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love” (Galatians 5:13).

Verse 18 holds two pictures. The BSB says believers ‘reflect’ the glory of the Lord, like a mirror. The Greek word can also mean to look at something as in a mirror, and some translations say ‘beholding’. Either way, believers stand before the Lord with nothing hiding their faces. And they are being changed. The Greek word is metamorphoō, from which English gets ‘metamorphosis’, the change of a caterpillar into a butterfly. It is the word used for Jesus being transfigured on the mountain (Matthew 17:2). The Greek says, word for word, ‘from glory into glory’. The BSB gives the sense as ‘with intensifying glory’: a change that goes on, step by step, until believers are like Christ.
passages.ot:
Paul is reading Exodus 34 closely. “When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face” (Exodus 34:33). “But whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with Him, he would remove the veil until he came out” (Exodus 34:34).

Moses had asked to see God's glory: “Please show me Your glory” (Exodus 33:18). God answered that no one could see his face and live (Exodus 33:20). Paul says the glory of God is now seen ‘in the face of Jesus Christ’ (4:6).

The Old Testament knows that hearts can be closed, and it also knows that God can open them. Moses told Israel, “Yet to this day the LORD has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear” (Deuteronomy 29:4). And a psalm prays, “Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law” (Psalm 119:18).

‘Freedom’ recalls the promise of Isaiah: the Spirit-anointed servant comes “to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners” (Isaiah 61:1). And ‘His image’ recalls the beginning: “So God created man in His own image” (Genesis 1:27). The Spirit is restoring that image.
passages.hard:
Is Paul showing contempt for the law of Moses, or for the Jewish people, when he speaks of a veil over their hearts?

No, and this must be said plainly, because these verses have been misused. For centuries some Christians used ‘the veil’ to look down on Jewish people, to mock them as blind, and to justify contempt and worse. That reading is false, and this site rejects it.

Look at what Paul actually says. He calls the old covenant glorious. He does not say Moses was wrong or the law was evil. He speaks as a Jew, of his own people, whom he loved. In Romans he writes, “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” for them (Romans 9:2), and “Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation” (Romans 10:1). He insists, “I am an Israelite myself” (Romans 11:1). Romans 9 to 11 shows that his words come with grief and hope, not scorn.

And the veil is not a final verdict. It is something that is ‘taken away’. Paul had worn it himself until he met Christ. He says it is lifted ‘whenever anyone turns to the Lord’, and the same could be said of any reader, of any people, who comes to Scripture without Christ. Nothing in these verses gives anyone a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people. As the site's notes on Acts 2 and Romans 11 say, such contempt has no ground in the New Testament.

One more thing. Paul says the veil lies over the reading of the old covenant, not over the old covenant itself. The Old Testament is not set aside. Read in the light of Christ, it remains Christian Scripture. Jesus himself, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets”, explained “what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself” (Luke 24:27).
passages.asks: Paul says believers are being changed, step by step, as they look to the Lord. Ask what you have been looking at most. Ask where you see that slow change in yourself, and where you are still waiting for it. And when you open the Old Testament, ask the Lord to take away whatever veil keeps you from seeing him there.
